The Chacoan horned frog, Ceratophrys cranwelli, is an iconic sit-and-wait predator of the South American Gran Chaco, renowned for its disproportionately large mouth and aggressive temperament. Upon hatching from a gelatinous egg mass, the emerging larva is initially lecithotrophic, sustained entirely by the endogenous yolk absorbed during the embryonated egg stage. The wet weight at birth from the egg is a scant 0.0049 grams [Wwb = 0.0049 grams], reflecting the modest egg diameter typical of the genus. The free-swimming tadpole then begins a period of rapid somatic growth as an actively growing larva, before reaching an allometric shift during amphibian metamorphosis. The wet weight at metamorphosis, marking the completion of tail resorption and the terrestrial transition into a post-metamorphic juvenile, has been recorded at 5.727 grams . This substantial increase in mass during larval development, a difference of over three orders of magnitude, underscores the extreme trophic efficiency of the aquatic larva as it exploits ephemeral ponds.

Female Chacoan horned frogs attain a significantly larger ultimate body size than males, a pattern consistent with sexual size dimorphism observed across many anurans where fecundity selection favors larger females. Comprehensive field surveys and captive rearing studies indicate that the ultimate snout-vent length (SVL) for females reaches 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], while males achieve a more modest final length of 10.8 centimeters [Li = 10.8 centimeters]. This divergence in asymptotic size is also reflected in the maximum adult body masses. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 500 grams [Wwi = 500 grams], making them among the heaviest amphibians in their range, whereas the ultimate wet weight for males is approximately 387 grams [Wwi = approximately 387 grams]. The functional significance of this disparity likely lies in the volume required for oocyte production, as a larger female body cavity can accommodate larger clutch masses, directly influencing reproductive output.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species is tied to a specific body size threshold rather than strictly to chronological age, a common pattern in indeterminate growers. For females, snout-vent length at puberty is approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters], at which point individuals are considered sub-adults capable of initiating gametogenesis. Reaching this size typically requires a period of sustained feeding, as the frog must accumulate sufficient lipid stores to support the high energetic costs associated with egg production. Under optimal thermal conditions, specifically at a stable environmental temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is a function of both clutch size and spawning frequency. A single large clutch can contain up to approximately 2100 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 2100 eggs per reproductive event], and females can produce a new clutch approximately every 96 days [F_R_i = clutch approximately every 96 days], resulting in an extremely high potential annual output of around 8000 eggs.

Longevity data for Ceratophrys cranwelli, derived from both field-based mark-recapture studies and long-term captive husbandry records, indicate a remarkable lifespan for an amphibian of this body size. The maximum recorded lifespan for individuals maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is 10 years [am = 10 years], a duration that distinguishes it from many small-bodied anurans that rarely survive more than a few seasons in the wild. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances the risks of desiccation in the arid Chaco against the advantages of intermittent reproductive opportunities following unpredictable rainfall events. During drought periods, the frogs estivate in a subterranean cocoon, dramatically reducing their metabolic rate and conserving body water, which allows them to defer mortality and extend their overall demographic window. The ability to persist for a decade under favorable captive regimes suggests that wild individuals, facing disease and predation, still achieve substantial ages when conditions permit.

Comparative physiological studies within the genus Ceratophrys highlight the pronounced effects of temperature on metabolic processes and development. At the species' preferred active body temperature range, around 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum rate of egg production can be sustained, as enzymatic and cellular machinery operate near their thermal optima. The endogenous lipid stores of the yolk-sac larva are depleted rapidly at this temperature, driving the early onset of exogenous feeding. The approximately 5.727 gram  mass at the larval-juvenile transition represents the culmination of a period of extremely rapid biomass accumulation, during which the tadpole converts abundant ephemeral resources into permanent tissue. These froglets immediately begin foraging on small invertebrates, a strategy that supports the rapid mass gain necessary to reach the juvenile stage. The ability of these juveniles to double in size within weeks is critical for surviving their first seasonal dry-down, when the terrestrial juvenile must locate suitable burrows to avoid lethal desiccation.
